title: Herod's laughter (Luke 23:1–12)
hook: sent to Herod, he says nothing, and two enemies become friends that day

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rooster, a fire, and the Lord turned and looked. Your line was the lord looked at peter. Who did you try to look at with kindness instead of blame? Day five hundred eighty-three.

Morning. The council brings Jesus to Pilate, the Roman governor, with charges that would worry any Roman: he stirs up the nation, forbids paying taxes to Caesar, calls himself a king. Luke's readers have already heard him on taxes: render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Pilate asks one question and announces: "I find no fault in this man." But they keep pressing. He started in Galilee, they say. Galilee. Pilate hears a way out. Galilee belongs to Herod, and Herod happens to be in Jerusalem at the time. Send the problem across town.
screen: `I FIND NO FAULT IN THIS MAN.`

segments.voice: This is Herod the tetrarch, ruler of Galilee. Earlier in Luke he's the man who says he beheaded John the Baptist, and Jesus once called him that fox. Herod is thrilled. Luke says he'd wanted to see Jesus for a long time, and hoped to see him do a miracle. Herod fires questions, many words, the King James says. And then: "he answered him nothing." Nothing. Jesus has talked his whole way through this Gospel, to crowds, to sinners, to Pharisees at dinner, and soon to a thief on a cross. Before this man he goes silent. Some readers hear an echo of Isaiah's servant, brought as a lamb to the slaughter, who opened not his mouth. The chief priests and scribes stand by, accusing him hard. So Herod and his soldiers turn to mockery. They treat him with contempt, laugh at him, dress him in a gorgeous robe like a costume king, and send him back to Pilate. Then Luke adds a strange, bitter line found in no other Gospel: "And the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together: for before they were at enmity between themselves." Two rulers who couldn't stand each other find common ground in a joke at the expense of a silent man. Luke doesn't explain the silence. Some readers hear dignity: some questions don't deserve an answer. Others hear refusal: he will not perform for a ruler who only wants a show. Either way, the miracle Herod hoped for never comes.

Here's the practice: stay silent before mockery. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you get baited: a comment section, a relative who likes to poke, a coworker's jokes. Picture the moment the jab lands. Notice the heat that rises, the reply forming in your mouth. Now imagine just letting the moment pass. Not sulking, not plotting. Simply not performing. Breathe through it. If you pray, you can ask God for that kind of quiet. The bell holds the time.
Herod's laughter. The ruler who wanted a miracle got silence, and answered it with mockery and a borrowed robe.
Your line: he answered nothing. Today, when someone baits you for a show, let one jab go by without answering it. Day five hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Churches that follow a three-year cycle of readings hear Luke's account of the trial, Herod's scene included, on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke; some readers connect Jesus's silence with the servant of Isaiah 53.

original.note: Greek: treating as nothing, with contempt. what Herod does to Jesus in Luke 23:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: Herod laughed at Jesus.
what it means: a ruler who wanted a show met silence, and turned it into mockery; and two enemies became friends over it.
what a scholar hears: only Luke has the hearing before Herod, the tetrarch who had beheaded John the Baptist, and some hear in the silence Isaiah's servant who opened not his mouth.

notes: The title 'Herod's laughter' is the index's; Luke 23:11 says Herod 'set him at nought, and mocked him'. The script describes mockery and laughter together.
Herod Antipas as son of Herod the Great; beheaded John (Luke 9:9); 'that fox' (Luke 13:32). Confirm.
Hook: 'earlier that week' places the Luke 20 teaching in the same week as the trial; Luke gives no exact day count. Confirm.
Original ἐξουθενήσας (Luke 23:11). Confirm form and accent.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Luke does not name Antipas or call him son of Herod the Great, and does not say Herod came 'for the feast' (23:7 'at that time'), so both are cut; 'earlier that week' became 'already heard him'; 'Christians have long heard' softened; fixed a muddled 'surrender ... will not perform' contrast; Good Friday reads John's Passion, which has no Herod scene, so howItsDone now names Palm Sunday in Luke's year; Herod is a tetrarch, so the fork says ruler, not king.
